signals.why_it_matters: Verified quiet: reconciliation ties to the pound against Table 1's 31.03.26 estimate; no LOBOs, no other market debt, no OLTL disclosed. 'We read it and nothing alarms' is a real product output for a district paper on this scale.

signals.headline: CFR grows £20.193m → £27.630m across 2025-2029 (+36.8%); the paper carries no new external borrowing and asks internal borrowing to do all the work (£17.364m → £25.309m, +45.8%)
signals.why_it_matters: Para 3.2 sets internal borrowing as the deliberate strategy. Table 1 shows external borrowing declining every year on natural annuity amortisation. Every additional £ of CFR is funded from cash — a stance that becomes harder to maintain as the investment book contracts (see net_investments).

signals.headline: Asset benchmark closes on £0.270m by 31.03.29 on the paper's own forecast; net investments contract from £36.8m to £12.6m over the same period
signals.why_it_matters: Paper explicitly runs an asset benchmark rather than a liability benchmark (para 3.7) because it 'does not have a borrowing requirement'. That reasoning stops holding on the paper's own 2029 figure. Chart on page 3 shows a modest recovery to about £5m by 2035 but the trough is inside the strategy period.

officer.subject: Your loan book ties to the pound — and where your asset benchmark lands in 2029
officer.body:
Hi,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on Appendix F, the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council on 26 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is unusually clean and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The reconciliation is the first thing worth saying. Table 1's external borrowing estimate at 31 March 2026 is £2,705k. Our file holds one PWLB loan against Havant — the annuity PW499449 drawn on 4.04%, currently sitting at £2,705,767 with a March 2042 maturity. That ties to £767. Your paragraph 12.1 gives the drafting-date figure of £2.76m, and the annuity amortisation between the two dates lines up. It is not often we can say the whole loan book reconciles on the pound — most books we read have twenty or two hundred loans and something drifts. The break cost on that one loan, priced off the DMO's premature repayment curve, is an indicative £141k discount today (about 5.2% of principal) — indicative only, and the DMO's quote is the only binding one.

The line that jumped out is Table 2 and paragraph 3.7. Havant is the only paper we've read this year that runs an asset benchmark rather than a liability benchmark, and the reasoning — 'the Council does not have a borrowing requirement' — is stated plainly. What Table 2 also shows is that same benchmark closing across the strategy period: £25.017m in 2025, £19.013m in 2026, £4.894m by 2027, £2.799m in 2028, and £270k by 31 March 2029. The chart on page 3 shows a modest recovery toward £5m by 2035, so the trough sits inside the strategy period rather than beyond it. That £270k point is arithmetically where the paper's own framing changes shape. Whether it changes anything about the strategy in practice is a decision for you — we don't offer a view — but it is a number worth having in front of members when the mid-year report comes back.

The mechanics behind that are consistent with paragraph 3.2's under-borrowing stance. CFR grows £20.2m to £27.6m across the same four years (+37%). External borrowing declines on natural annuity amortisation. Internal borrowing is asked to do all the work of financing the CFR growth (£17.4m to £25.3m, +46%), and it does so out of a contracting investment book — Table 1 has net investments falling from £36.8m to £12.6m over the same window. The interactive liability benchmark pathway at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark takes your figures as a comparator against the councils we've read that are running the more usual frame — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes.

Paragraph 12.4 flags that short rates have fallen and that internal or short-dated borrowing looks more cost-effective over the medium term. The dashboard at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard shows the certainty rate at each fixing today, so it takes about ten seconds to see how the current curve compares with the assumption behind that paragraph. And paragraph 12.10's reference to forward-starting loans is a real option — the monthly PWLB draw data at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows how the sector is currently using them.

None of it needs a meeting or a subscription. On training, three look most relevant given the shape of your paper: our liability benchmark pathway (interactive, built on live data, and the natural comparator for the asset benchmark you run); Interest rate risk, for the cost-of-carry conversation at §12.6; and Debt rescheduling, for the discount you would face on the one loan if the question ever came up. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
